LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- A crowd of about 10,000 came to Dodger Stadium on Saturday, but they weren't there for a baseball game. Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shakes hands with recruiter Raul Mendez from L.A. County Probation Department. While the Dodgers were in Arizona for spring training, more than 80 employers set up employment booths in the parking lot just beyond the center field fence. To those who turned out, finding a job would be a home run. Participating companies included Coca-Cola, Lowe's and Union Bank. And government agencies including the FBI, the Social Security Administration and the Army Corps of Engineers  were there, too. All had one thing in common: They were hiring. And that was music to the ears of 30-year-old Eric Clardy. It has been a rough couple of years for Clardy. He was laid off from his job as a loan processor when the real estate market started to tank. Then, after finding work as a project manager for a plumbing company, layoffs struck again. "It's kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want," he said. Clardy said his goal is to make contact with at least 10 potential employers a day via phone, letters and the Internet. Being unemployed is hard work, too.  Watch how Clardy goes about trying to find a job » . "It was a scramble," Clardy said. "I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs." The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday's event, which they said drew about 10,000 people. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair to fill some 500 part-time jobs at the stadium during baseball season drew about 7,000 applicants. California's unemployment rate is 10.1 percent, a full 2 percentage points higher than the national rate. The state's Employment Development office estimates that nearly a half-million state residents have lost their jobs in the past year. "We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago," said Gloria Bratton Moore, who runs the state-funded Work Source job center in Los Angeles. Nonetheless, she said, "There are jobs available." But at Dodger Stadium, it was clear that competition for those available jobs is stiff. Applicants were often stacked four and five people deep in front of employer tables, and there was little chance for most of the 10,000 job seekers to make much of an impression. But organizers worked hard to pump up any flagging spirits. "Yes we can. Yes we can," Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia chanted over a loudspeaker. State lawmaker Kevin deLeon told the crowd that they are among the nation's hardest-hit in this economic downturn, but he exhorted them to not give up. "We will get out of this economic funk," he said. "We will recover soon. We've got to have hope." Garcia and deLeon's comments echoed the campaign slogans of President Obama, who recently won approval of a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package. Recruiters from the government agencies present at the job fair said that money will start creating jobs within the next few months. The Army Corps of Engineers told applicants that it is hiring for a wide variety of positions, including those for engineers, heavy-equipment operators and environmental field workers. The Commerce Department is adding more than 1 million jobs in preparation of the 2010 census, and other federal agencies are hiring as well. All of that was good news to Clardy, who left resumes and filled out applications at a number of the 80 booths cluttering the stadium's parking lot. But he remained realistic about this day's activities leading directly to a job. "It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview," he said. "Now it doesn't seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore."

# Job Seekers Flock to Dodger Stadium in Search of Employment, Not Baseball

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- A crowd of roughly 10,000 gathered at Dodger Stadium on Saturday, though not for a baseball game. While the Dodgers trained in Arizona, more than 80 employers set up recruitment booths in the parking lot beyond the center field fence, transforming the venue into a job fair. For the attendees, landing a position would indeed feel like a home run.

Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shakes hands with recruiter Raul Mendez of the Los Angeles County Probation Department.

Participating companies included Coca-Cola, Lowe's, and Union Bank, alongside government agencies such as the FBI, the Social Security Administration, and the Army Corps of Engineers. All shared a common purpose: they were hiring—welcome news to 30-year-old Eric Clardy.

The past couple of years have been difficult for Clardy. He was laid off from his position as a loan processor when the real estate market began to falter. After securing work as a project manager for a plumbing company, he was laid off once again.

"It's kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start working toward the career you really want," he explained.

Clardy said his goal is to reach out to at least ten potential employers daily through phone calls, letters, and online applications. Unemployment, he noted, is its own form of labor.

"It was a scramble," Clardy said. "I was selling insurance, taking temp jobs, going to job fairs."

The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday's event, which drew an estimated 10,000 attendees. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair aimed at filling roughly 500 part-time positions at the stadium during baseball season attracted nearly 7,000 applicants.

California's unemployment rate currently stands at 10.1 percent—a full two percentage points above the national average. The state's Employment Development Department estimates that nearly half a million residents have lost their jobs over the past year.

"We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago," said Gloria Bratton Moore, who oversees the state-funded WorkSource job center in Los Angeles. Still, she added, "There are jobs available."

At Dodger Stadium, however, competition for those openings was evident. Applicants often queued four or five deep at employer tables, leaving little opportunity for most of the 10,000 job seekers to make a lasting impression.

Organizers nonetheless worked to keep spirits high. "Yes we can. Yes we can," chanted Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia over a loudspeaker. State lawmaker Kevin de León told the crowd that, while they are among the hardest hit by the economic downturn, they should not lose hope.

"We will get out of this economic funk," he said. "We will recover soon. We've got to have hope."

The remarks from Garcia and de León echoed the rhetoric of President Obama, who recently secured approval for a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package. Recruiters from government agencies at the fair noted that this funding is expected to generate jobs within the coming months. The Army Corps of Engineers, for instance, said it is hiring for a range of roles, including engineers, heavy-equipment operators, and environmental field workers. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department plans to add more than a million positions in preparation for the 2010 census, with other federal agencies expanding their workforces as well.

This was encouraging news for Clardy, who distributed resumes and completed applications at numerous booths scattered throughout the stadium's parking lot. Still, he remained pragmatic about the day's prospects.

"It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview," he said. "Now it doesn't seem like that. Some companies aren't even taking resumes at job fairs anymore."

# Los Angeles: The City of Angels

Los Angeles, often abbreviated as L.A., is the largest city in the state of California and the second-largest city in the United States by population. Nestled along the Pacific coast in Southern California, this sprawling metropolis is renowned worldwide for its diverse culture, entertainment industry, and iconic landmarks.

## A Global Entertainment Capital

Los Angeles is synonymous with the film and television industry. Hollywood, a neighborhood within the city, has served as the historic center of American cinema for over a century. Major studios, production companies, and countless talented individuals from around the world converge here, making it a global hub for entertainment and media production.

## Geography and Climate

Situated in a coastal basin surrounded by mountains, Los Angeles enjoys a Mediterranean climate characterized by warm, dry summers and mild winters. The city stretches across a vast area, encompassing diverse neighborhoods from the beaches of Santa Monica and Venice to the hills of Beverly Hills and the urban core of Downtown LA.

## Cultural Diversity

One of California's most vibrant cities, Los Angeles is home to a remarkably diverse population representing cultures from around the globe. This diversity is reflected in its neighborhoods, cuisine, festivals, and daily life, making it one of the most multicultural cities in the world.

## Economic Significance

Beyond entertainment, Los Angeles boasts a robust economy spanning technology, international trade, fashion, tourism, and manufacturing. The Port of Los Angeles is one of the busiest shipping ports in the country, reflecting the city's importance as a gateway for Pacific trade.

## Conclusion

Los Angeles, California, remains a dynamic and influential city that continues to shape global culture, entertainment, and innovation. Its unique blend of natural beauty, economic opportunity, and cultural richness ensures its status as one of the world's most fascinating urban centers.

# Thousands Line Up at Dodger Stadium for Massive Job Fair as Unemployment Crisis Deepens

**LOS ANGELES, California** — Long before the gates opened Tuesday morning, the line outside Dodger Stadium stretched for more than a mile, snaking through parking lots normally reserved for baseball fans. But there was no game today — just thousands of Southern Californians desperate for work.

An estimated 10,000 job seekers descended on the iconic stadium for one of the largest job fairs the region has seen since the recession began, as California's unemployment rate climbed to 12.3 percent, well above the national average.

"I've been out of work for eight months," said Maria Delgado, 34, a former administrative assistant who arrived at 4 a.m. to secure a spot near the front of the line. "I have two kids at home. I'll wait as long as it takes."

By the time doors opened at 8 a.m., the line had grown so long that some job seekers said they walked nearly two miles just to reach the end of it. Stadium officials, accustomed to managing crowds for Dodgers games, said they had never seen turnout like this for anything other than opening day.

Organizers had expected a few thousand attendees. Instead, they got a crowd more befitting a playoff game — only this time, everyone was hoping to walk away with something far more valuable than a souvenir: a paycheck.

Inside, roughly 100 employers set up booths across the stadium's concourse and field level, offering positions ranging from retail and hospitality to nursing, trucking, and government work. Representatives from companies like UPS, Kaiser Permanente, and several county agencies fielded résumés by the thousands.

"We brought 500 applications with us. We ran out by 10:30," said one recruiter for a Southern California healthcare provider, who declined to give her name. "The need out there is just overwhelming."

Economists say the scene at Dodger Stadium is a stark illustration of the human toll of the downturn, which has wiped out millions of jobs nationwide since the recession began. Los Angeles County alone has shed hundreds of thousands of positions in industries ranging from construction to manufacturing to entertainment.

"This isn't just about statistics anymore," said Dr. Elena Vasquez, an economist at a local university who visited the fair to observe. "You're looking at people who did everything right — got an education, built a career — and now they're standing in line for hours just for the chance to hand someone a résumé."

For many attendees, the day was as much about morale as employment. Support groups and financial counselors set up informational tables alongside the corporate booths, offering guidance on unemployment benefits, mortgage assistance, and stress management.

James Whitfield, 52, said he had been laid off from a mid-level management job at an aerospace firm nearly a year ago. He arrived at the stadium wearing his best — and only — remaining suit.

"You lose more than a paycheck when you lose your job," Whitfield said, standing in the shadow of the stadium's iconic scoreboard. "You lose your sense of purpose. Coming here, seeing all these people in the same boat — it helps, honestly. But it's also heartbreaking."

By early afternoon, stadium officials said thousands were still waiting outside, with some being turned away as booths ran low on materials and staff. City officials indicated they were already planning additional job fairs in the coming months, citing overwhelming demand.

As the sun set over Chavez Ravine, the line outside the stadium had finally dwindled — but for many of those who had spent the day waiting, hoping, and handing over résumés, the outcome remained uncertain.

"I don't know if I'll get a call back," Delgado said, folding a stack of business cards into her purse as she left. "But at least today, I felt like I was doing something."

*CNN will continue to follow developments as unemployment figures are released next month.*

# Job Seekers Flock to Sacramento Career Fair as Unemployment Concerns Persist

**SACRAMENTO, Calif.** — Hundreds of job seekers lined up outside the Sacramento Convention Center early Tuesday morning, some arriving more than an hour before doors opened, as local employers gathered for one of the region's largest job fairs this year.

The event, hosted by the California Employment Development Department (EDD) in partnership with the Sacramento Chamber of Commerce, drew more than 60 employers spanning healthcare, logistics, technology, and hospitality sectors.

## Long Lines, Longer Waits for Work

By 9 a.m., the line stretched around the block. Attendees carried folders of printed résumés, dressed in business attire despite the summer heat.

Maria Gonzalez, 34, a former administrative assistant who was laid off in March, was among the first in line.

"I've applied to probably 150 jobs online in the past four months and heard back from maybe five," Gonzalez said. "Being here, actually talking to a real person — it feels different. More hopeful, even if nothing comes of it today."

James Whitfield, 52, who spent two decades in manufacturing before his plant closed last year, expressed frustration mixed with determination.

"At my age, you start to wonder if anyone wants to hire you," Whitfield said. "But I've got skills. I just need someone to give me a chance to show it."

## Employers Say They're Hiring — But Selectively

Representatives from companies attending the fair described a competitive labor market, with many roles receiving high volumes of applicants.

"We're not seeing a shortage of candidates — if anything, we're seeing an abundance," said Priya Patel, a recruiter with a regional healthcare provider. "The challenge is finding the right fit quickly. Events like this help us have real conversations instead of just sorting through résumés online."

Several logistics and warehouse companies said they had immediate openings, while tech firms in attendance noted they were primarily hiring for specialized roles, leaving many entry-level tech job seekers without direct matches.

## Officials Point to Broader Economic Trends

California's unemployment rate has remained above the national average in recent months, according to the state EDD, driven partly by layoffs in tech, retail, and government sectors.

"We know these numbers represent real people and real struggles," said EDD spokesperson Daniel Reyes. "Job fairs like this one are just one tool, but they matter because they create direct human connections between employers and job seekers who might otherwise never cross paths."

Reyes added that the state has expanded resources for retraining programs, particularly for workers transitioning out of declining industries.

"We're seeing displaced workers from sectors like retail and manufacturing needing to pivot into growth areas — healthcare, skilled trades, renewable energy," he said. "That transition takes time and support."

## Mixed Emotions, Cautious Optimism

By early afternoon, some attendees left with callback promises; others left uncertain.

Gonzalez said she had two follow-up interviews scheduled for later in the week. "It's not a job yet," she said, "but it's the most hopeful I've felt in months."

Whitfield was less certain about his prospects but said he planned to attend the next fair regardless.

"You keep showing up," he said. "That's all you can do."

---

*The EDD said additional job fairs are planned across the state in the coming weeks as officials continue efforts to connect job seekers with employers amid ongoing economic uncertainty.*

---

# Thousands Line Up at LA Job Fair as Residents Seek Economic Relief

**LOS ANGELES** — Before dawn broke over the Los Angeles Convention Center on Wednesday, the line had already stretched for three city blocks. By 8 a.m., organizers estimated more than 4,000 job seekers were waiting to enter what has become one of the largest employment fairs the city has hosted in recent memory.

The event, organized by the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation in partnership with the mayor's office, brought together more than 150 employers spanning healthcare, logistics, hospitality, and manufacturing sectors. For many attendees, it represented not just an opportunity, but a last resort after months of fruitless searching.

## "I've Applied to Over 200 Places"

Marcus Delgado, 34, arrived at 5:30 a.m. wearing his only remaining suit, a relic from his previous job as a warehouse operations manager before his employer shuttered its Southern California distribution center in the spring.

"I've applied to over 200 places since February," Delgado said, adjusting a folder of resumes tucked under his arm. "Some days you send out applications and hear absolutely nothing back. Not even a rejection email. It messes with your head after a while."

Delgado, who supports two children, said he'd exhausted his unemployment benefits weeks ago and had taken on gig delivery work to cover rent. "This isn't what I trained for, but you do what you have to do," he said. "Today, I'm just hoping somebody looks at my resume and sees more than a gap in employment. I built a whole logistics operation before things fell apart. That has to count for something."

By midday, Delgado said he'd had three promising conversations, including one with a regional distribution company that asked him to come in for a formal interview next week. "It's not a job yet," he said, "but it's the first time in months I've felt like maybe things are turning around."

## City Officials Respond to Economic Pressure

The turnout reflects broader anxieties about the region's economic trajectory. Los Angeles County's unemployment rate has hovered above state averages in recent months, driven partly by contraction in entertainment production, retail closures, and softening in the logistics sector that once buoyed the local economy.

City Councilmember Elena Ruiz, whose district includes several neighborhoods hit hardest by recent layoffs, walked the convention floor Wednesday morning, stopping to speak with job seekers and employer representatives alike.

"When you see a line like this, stretching around the block before sunrise, it's a gut check," Ruiz said. "These are our neighbors, people who want to work, who are qualified, who are hustling every single day. Our job as elected officials is to make sure the infrastructure exists so opportunity actually reaches them."

Ruiz pointed to a recently passed city initiative offering tax incentives to companies that commit to hiring locally, calling events like Wednesday's fair "necessary, but not sufficient" on their own.

"A job fair gets people in the room," she said. "But we need sustained investment—workforce training programs, transit access to job centers, childcare support so parents can actually take these interviews. Otherwise we're just treating the symptom."

Mayor's office spokesperson David Chen, representing the administration at the event, struck a similarly measured tone. "We're proud to help facilitate this kind of connection between employers and residents," Chen said. "But we're not going to pretend a single day solves systemic issues. The mayor is pushing for expanded job training funding in next year's budget specifically because we know demand like this isn't going away."

## Employers See Opportunity Amid Challenge

For companies at the fair, the turnout offered a silver lining. Representatives from a major regional healthcare provider said they'd collected over 300 resumes by early afternoon, far exceeding expectations.

"There's incredible talent here," said hiring coordinator Priya Nair. "People who are motivated, who show up ready. It's honestly a reminder of how much this city has to offer if the right connections get made."

Still, for job seekers like Delgado, the day carried mixed emotions—hope tempered by the visible scale of need surrounding him.

"You look around and see thousands of people just like you," he said, glancing at the line still snaking outside as afternoon wore on. "Part of you feels less alone. Another part wonders if there's really enough out there for everybody."

As the fair wound down Wednesday evening, organizers said they were already planning a follow-up event for next month, citing overwhelming demand as justification. Whether that demand reflects a temporary rough patch or a deeper structural shift in the region's job market remains a question City Hall will be grappling with well beyond this week.

*Reporting contributed by staff correspondents covering the Los Angeles labor market.*

# Thousands Line Up for Jobs at Stadium Career Fair Amid Economic Downturn

**FOXBOROUGH, Mass. (AP)** — By 6 a.m., the parking lots surrounding Gillette Stadium were already filling with cars, their headlights cutting through the pre-dawn darkness as thousands of job seekers arrived hours before the doors would open.

By the time organizers unlocked the entrance at 9 a.m., the line stretched more than a quarter-mile around the stadium's perimeter, a sea of business suits, resumes tucked under arms, and faces etched with a mixture of hope and exhaustion.

The job fair, one of the largest held in New England since the recession deepened last year, drew an estimated 8,000 job seekers competing for positions with roughly 75 employers — a ratio that underscored the brutal math facing American workers as unemployment climbed toward 10 percent nationally.

"I've been out of work for fourteen months," said Marcus Chen, 34, a former mortgage industry analyst from Worcester who arrived at the stadium at 4:30 a.m. to secure a spot near the front of the line. "I have two kids. I've applied to probably 300 jobs. This is the first time I've felt like maybe, just maybe, something might happen today."

Chen was far from alone. Nearby, Patricia Alvarez, 52, stood clutching a folder of resumes, some fifteen years removed from the last time she'd needed to look for work.

"I was a bookkeeper for the same company for eighteen years," Alvarez said. "Then in March, they just told us — no warning — that we were all being let go. I never thought I'd be standing in a line like this at my age."

The scene inside the stadium's concourse resembled a strange hybrid of a career expo and a rock concert queue, with folding tables replacing merchandise booths and human resources representatives standing in for vendors. Companies ranging from healthcare providers to logistics firms to a handful of financial services companies set up modest booths, each swarmed within minutes by anxious applicants.

Representatives from CVS Caremark, one of the few employers actively hiring in significant numbers, said they received more than 1,200 applications within the first three hours alone.

"We're humbled, honestly," said Diane Marsh, a regional recruiter for the pharmacy chain. "We have positions to fill, but nothing close to the volume of people who need them. It's overwhelming to see how many qualified, desperate people are out there."

Massachusetts' unemployment rate stood at 8.9 percent in the month leading up to the fair, mirroring a grim national trend that saw more than 15 million Americans out of work. Economists have described the downturn — rooted in the collapse of the housing market and ensuing financial crisis — as the most severe since the Great Depression.

State Labor Secretary Suzanne Bump, who toured the event, acknowledged the scale of the challenge.

"Events like this are important, but let's be honest about what they represent," Bump said. "We have thousands of skilled, hardworking people chasing far too few opportunities. That's not a reflection of their effort. It's a reflection of the economy we're all still climbing out of."

For many attendees, the day brought mixed results. Some walked away with promising leads or scheduled interviews. Others left with little more than a stack of business cards and a renewed sense of uncertainty.

James Whitfield, 45, a laid-off construction supervisor, said he'd attended four job fairs in the past six months.

"You start to recognize the same faces," Whitfield said, gesturing toward the crowd. "We're all in the same boat. I keep telling myself something's going to break eventually. I just don't know when."

By early afternoon, as the crowds began to thin and vendors packed away their banners, the parking lots that had filled before sunrise slowly emptied once more — job seekers dispersing back into a job market that, for now, showed little sign of easing.

"We'll be back next time," Alvarez said, folding her now-empty resume folder under her arm. "What choice do we have?"
